transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-01-15
Start: 14:30 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Olivia Park (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Samir Gomez (Redwood SE), Leah Martinez (Cascade CTO), Aaron Blake (Infra), Priya Singh (ML Eng), Tom Hsu (Prod)

Summary:
Quick kickoff focused on POC scoping for capacity sizing and autoscaling. Customer wants a two-week pilot that validates reserved GPU baseline with configured burst capacity and deterministic fallback rules to cheaper models/regions. Primary success criteria: maintain p95 latency under 250ms for short completions (<=64 tokens) and keep cost within target (~$0.004 per 1k tokens effective) while handling traffic spikes up to 3x baseline.

Topics covered:
- Current traffic patterns and where Cascade expects spikes (batch job ingestion 02:00 UTC + interactive peak 16:00 local).
- Baseline model choice (Llama-3-8B-like open backbone vs a quantized 4-bit variant).
- Reserved GPU sizing, burst buffer (GPU pool + ephemeral GPUs), and autoscale policies (min/target/max, warm pools).
- Fallback policies: model downgrades, region failover, queued request handling and graceful degradation (partial responses, short-circuiting).
- Benchmarks needed: latency distribution (p50/p95/p99), tokens/sec, memory/kv cache hit rates, and cost-per-token under different quantization/batching configs.
- Timeline and deliverables for the two-week POC.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Olivia Park: hey everyone, thanks for joining; we've got about 40 minutes — goal is to align on success criteria and the capacity plan for the poc. i'll run through a rough approach and ravi will add the perf pieces.
[00:12] Leah Martinez: great — thanks. quick background: we're building a customer-facing rec sys that uses short prompts mostly, average 24 tokens, but we do have long sessions for debugging where up to 1k tokens can be generated. our primary concern is latency during interactive peak and controlling cost cause margins are tight.
[00:33] Aaron Blake: yeah and infra-wise we run in a single cloud region eu-west-1 for now. we do have an agreement to add a secondary region later. security-wise we need audit logs and KMS integration — but that's for the security review. today is sizing.
[00:45] Ravi Patel: perfect — two quick things we'll need: a token-length histogram and your QPS windows for a typical day and peak day. from that we can map to required GPU seconds and sizing. in the poc we often use a reserved baseline (1-2 gpus) plus a burst pool that seconds in on demand; that prevents cold-start spikes.
[01:08] Priya Singh: when you say burst pool, do you mean dedicated extra gpus reserved for the poc or on-demand? how does the fallback work if burst isn't available?
[01:20] Samir Gomez: good question — we usually propose reserved capacity that covers baseline 80% of your steady QPS. then we configure a burst policy that allows ephemeral capacity (short-lived) up to 3x the baseline for 10-15 minute windows. if burst is exhausted or unavailable, fallback policy kicks in — that includes routing to a cheaper quantized model (4-bit) or shifting to a lower-cost region, and optionally returning a short-circuit response with a note about degraded fidelity.
[01:51] Leah Martinez: that sounds sensible. what's the expected latency delta when we fallback to quantized 4-bit model?
[01:58] Ravi Patel: typically for short completions p95 you might see +20-40ms depending on batch sizes and kernel optimizations; in some cases if we downgrade model size (8B -> 3B) you could see lower latency but reduced quality. we recommend keeping a canary route to compare outputs against the primary model during the poc.
[02:20] Tom Hsu: for success criteria, we want hard limits: p95 < 250ms for <=64 tokens, and p99 < 600ms for longer sessions. also need to prove cost per 1k tokens with our sample workload.
[02:35] Olivia Park: noted — we'll bake those into the poc acceptance. for the sizing exercise here's an example calc: if your peak interactive QPS is 25 rps, avg tokens/req 24, that's 600 tokens/sec. on an A100-like GPU with our runtime you'd get ~3k tokens/sec single-GPU with batching for that model shape, so baseline of 1 GPU should be fine for steady load, but spikes up to 75 rps would need burst capacity or additional reserved.
[03:08] Aaron Blake: are those numbers measured with kv cache warm? our workload is very conversational and kv cache hit rate matters a lot.
[03:18] Ravi Patel: yes the numbers assume a warmed KV cache and steady sequence lengths. if you have cold starts frequently, you'll see a higher latency for the first requests. for the poc we suggest a short warmup trace before measuring.
[03:33] Priya Singh: what about batching? our UX needs low tail latency for interactive calls, batching hurts that sometimes.
[03:40] Samir Gomez: continuous batching is adaptive — it will target latency SLOs; you pick a target p95 and the runtime bounds batching accordingly. for the POC we'll show two configs: latency-first (very small batch windows, higher cost) and cost-first (longer batch windows, higher throughput).
[04:05] Leah Martinez: good. can you walk through fallback sequence? we want to avoid failing requests silently.
[04:12] Ravi Patel: fallback plan we propose: 1) Try reserved capacity in eu-west-1 primary. 2) If saturated, spin up burst ephemerals in same region if available. 3) If burst fails, route to quantized 4-bit model in same region. 4) If local capacity still not available, failover to second region (latency penalty). 5) Final fallback: queue requests with explanatory header and progressive partial responses. Each step is instrumented with latency/cost metrics and you can set thresholds to stop at any step.
[05:02] Aaron Blake: about step 4, cross-region failover — that impacts compliance and data residency. we need to flag that as optional and require a specific written approval for the poc.
[05:12] Olivia Park: understood — we'll mark cross-region failover as opt-in. for the benchmark matrix we'll include a column for compliance-friendly mode (no cross-region failover).
[05:28] Tom Hsu: timeline — we want pilot running by end of next week, is two weeks realistic for full benching?
[05:34] Samir Gomez: pilot spin-up (reserved baseline + burst config) can be done in 2-3 days once we have access and sample prompts. benchmark runs and analysis take another week; final acceptance and documentation another few days. two-week POC is doable.
[05:50] Priya Singh: what about cost modelling — can you show tradeoffs? e.g., 1 reserved GPU vs 2 reserved and no burst?
[05:58] Ravi Patel: yes we will run scenario sims: reserved-only, reserved+burst, and reserved+smaller model fallback. the capacity spreadsheet will show estimated $/1k tokens and daily cost based on your traffic histogram.
[06:12] Leah Martinez: for benchmarks, we expect you to run at least three passes: steady-state baseline, 3x spike for 15 mins to validate burst, and long-session memory stress for kv cache.
[06:22] Samir Gomez: agreed — and we'll capture p50/p95/p99, token/sec, batch sizes, and GPU utilization per run. we'll also provide the raw logs and a short analysis note about any regressions.
[06:35] Aaron Blake: are there any particular config knobs we'll need to change in our side like networking or VPC peering?
[06:42] Olivia Park: for Redwood Private or Dedicated, we'll need network rules for the control plane and maybe an egress path for metrics. for Hosted pilot we can use secure tunnels; we'll detail both in the onboarding doc.
[06:55] Priya Singh: can you do a short run on mixed sequence lengths so we can see the tail?
[07:00] Ravi Patel: yes that's part of the benchmark template — mixed lengths and conversational traces.
[07:07] Tom Hsu: what does success look like at the end of the two-week POC?
[07:12] Olivia Park: clear pass/fail criteria: 1) p95 < 250ms (<=64 tokens) across 3 steady runs; 2) burst policy shows capacity up to 3x baseline for 15-minute windows without exceeding p95 threshold by >30%; 3) cost-per-token within agreed tolerance; 4) documented fallback behavior and audit logs for failover events. if any of these fail we do an additional tuning sprint.
[07:38] Leah Martinez: sounds good. last question — can you show us how automatic KV prefix caching would change performance?
[07:46] Ravi Patel: absolutely — we'll include a cache-on prefix run vs non-cache run. typically you see big wins in tokens/sec and p95 when cache hit rates are high.
[07:58] Olivia Park: ok i'll capture the action items. we'll send the spreadsheet with a couple of scenarios and the benchmark template. any final questions?
[08:07] Priya Singh: none. thanks, excited to get going.
[08:10] Leah Martinez: thanks all.

Recap / next steps (spoken at end):
- Redwood to share capacity spreadsheet and benchmark template (Olivia)
- Customer to send token histogram and sample prompts (Priya)
- Redwood SE to prepare burst/fallback runbook and schedule benchmark run (Ravi)

End of recording.
